title: Assumptions, Inferences, and Courses of Action
tagline: Year 3 — What a statement takes for granted, what it lets you conclude, and what should be done about it

introduction.overview: Three related question types start from a short statement. An assumption is something the speaker takes for granted for the statement to make sense. An inference is something you can safely conclude from it. A course of action is a step that should be taken in response to a problem. The key is to keep them apart: assumptions sit behind the statement, inferences come out of it, and courses of action are about what to do next.
introduction.placementRelevance: These three types appear together in most logical-reasoning papers.
introduction.realWorldContext: Reading between the lines of a notice, a report or a plan, and deciding what to do about it, uses all three skills.

learningObjectives: Spot the assumption that must be true for a statement to make sense
Choose practical, relevant courses of action

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Assumption: unstated support. Inference: stated consequence. Course of action: proposed step.

coreDefinitions: Implicit assumption: a belief the speaker must hold, otherwise the statement would make no sense.
Inference: a conclusion that follows from the statement, possibly with common sense but without new facts.
Course of action: a practical step that deals with the problem in the statement.
Negation test: if denying the assumption makes the statement pointless, it is implicit.
Extreme options (ban all, close everything) are rarely correct.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: An assumption is the hidden bridge between what is said and why it was said. To test one, ask: if this were false, would the statement still make sense?
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: For assumptions use the negation test. For inferences stick to what the facts guarantee. For courses of action choose steps that are practical, targeted and proportionate.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Negation test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Deny the assumption; does the statement collapse?
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: "Phones may disturb others" denied: the notice is pointless

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Safe inference
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Only facts or arithmetic from the statement

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Proportion
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Fit the action to the problem

mainNarrative: Statement: "Please keep your mobile phones switched off during the film." The implicit assumption is that phones may disturb other viewers. The claim that everyone owns a phone is not needed: the request makes sense whether or not everyone has one.
A negation test confirms it. If phones could not disturb anyone, the request would be pointless. If not everyone has a phone, the request is still sensible.

Inferences must follow from the facts. "The factory produced 500 units in January and 600 in February" allows "production increased from January to February"; it does not allow "production will rise again in March".

For courses of action, first read the problem. "A large number of students were found suffering from dengue" calls for closing the college for a while and cleaning the premises. Telling students to stay at home and not worry does not deal with the cause.
Reject extremes and delay. "The water level in the main reservoir has fallen to a critical level" calls for rationing now, not for waiting for the monsoon.

deepDiveAspects.title: Assumption vs inference
deepDiveAspects.content: An assumption supports the statement from behind; an inference grows from it in front. The same sentence can be neither.

deepDiveAspects.title: Courses of action
deepDiveAspects.content: The best actions are specific, immediate and within the authority named in the statement.

solvedExamples.title: Assumption
solvedExamples.question: Statement: Buy a ticket in advance to avoid long queues at the museum. Assumption: Advance tickets are available. Is it implicit?

steps.title: Deny it
steps.explanation: If advance tickets were not available, the advice would be pointless.

solvedExamples.title: Inference
solvedExamples.question: Statement: A school has 600 students and 40% are girls. Which follows: there are 240 girls, or there are 400 boys?

solvedExamples.title: Course of action
solvedExamples.question: Statement: The water level in the city's main reservoir has fallen to a critically low level. Which is better: start rationing water now, or wait for the monsoon?

steps.title: Urgency
steps.explanation: The problem is current and serious.

steps.title: Choice
steps.explanation: Start rationing now; waiting is passive.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: It deals directly with the shortage.

shortcutMethods.title: Negate, compute, fit

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Assumption: negate it. Inference: compute or restate only. Course of action: pick the specific, proportionate step.

rulesForApplication: Match the action to the cause.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a prediction as an inference
Choosing a hidden fact as an assumption

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Eliminate options with words like all, never, ban, immediately close everything.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Underline the problem word in the statement.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Courses of action respond to the problem; assumptions support the statement.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I apply the negation test?
Can I choose a proportionate action?
